study.title: Numbers 3 - Levi in service, the firstborn to the LORD
study.overview: The chapter organizes the people around the sanctity of the tabernacle and the responsibility of worship. First, Aaron's priestly lineage is confirmed, with the solemn memory of Nadab and Abihu's death for offering strange fire. Then the Levites are separated to serve as auxiliaries of the priests and as a guard of the sanctuary, instead of the firstborn of Israel. Then the text details the counting of the Levitical families, their positions around the tabernacle and their specific functions in the transport and care of sacred objects. Finally, the count of the firstborn shows a surplus of 273 men, whose difference is redeemed in silver, and delivered to Aaron and his sons, according to the commandment of the LORD.

outline.title: Aaron's priestly lineage and the warning of judgment
outline.explanation: The verses present the sons of Aaron and establish that Eleazar and Ithamar continued in the priesthood after the death of Nadab and Abihu. The narrative emphasizes that access to sacred service is not casual: the holiness of God requires precise obedience, and the death of the two children functions as a permanent warning against the profanity of worship.

outline.title: Levites are given to the priesthood instead of the firstborn
outline.explanation: The LORD separates the tribe of Levi to assist Aaron and his sons, assuming tasks connected to the tabernacle. The basis of this substitution is redeeming: the firstborn belong to the LORD since the preservation of the firstborn in Israel at the exit of Egypt. Thus the Levites appear as a dedicated people, belonging to the Lord and placed in the service of the congregation.

outline.title: Counting and distribution of the Levitical families around the tabernacle
outline.explanation: Moses must count all the Levites men from one month of age, and the text lists Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, with their families and numbers. Each group receives a specific place in the camp and a concrete responsibility: some take care of the curtains and roofs, others of the ark, the table, the candlestick and the altars, and others of the boards, columns, bases and stakes. The organization shows order, distinction of functions and protection of holy space.

outline.title: The firstborn are counted and the difference is rescued in silver
outline.explanation: The LORD tells the firstborn men of Israel, and the total surpasses the number of Levites in 273. These surpluses must be rescued with five shekels per head, and the money is handed over to Aaron and his children. The procedure confirms that belonging to the LORD involves substitution, payment of ransom and administration according to the divine word.

study.context: The chapter is set in the wilderness of Sinai and directly depends on the organization of the worship revealed by God to Moses. The tabernacle is the center of the life of Israel, and the disposition of the Levitical tribes and families reflects the need to preserve the holiness of the space where God dwells among the people. The text also relies on the memorial of the exit from Egypt, when the firstborn were spared and came to belong to the Lord.
study.theology: Chapter theology revolves around holiness, mediation and substitution. The holiness of the LORD makes it impossible to treat worship as something common; therefore, access to sacred service is restricted, and the death of Nadab and Abiú shows the danger of disobedience. Aaron and his children exercise the priesthood as visible mediators, but the Levites are given to them to serve and protect the tabernacle, showing that God organizes his people with distinct functions. Moreover, the replacement of the firstborn by the Levites teaches that the life of Israel was preserved by grace and that all that was spared belongs to the Lord. The silver rescue reinforces that belonging to God has cost and that redemption is a central theme already in the community's own arrangement. In evangelical Christian reading, this substitution logic can be seen as a typological anticipation of Christ's work, without denying the immediate meaning of the text: one occupies the place of another and pays the price due.

scholarViews.insight: The surplus of 273 firstborn in relation to the Levites requires a ransom price of five pieces of silver per head, and this provision points to Christ as a substitute that pays the price of redemption for all mankind.

Aaron's family is confirmed in the priesthood, and the expression that the approaching foreigner will die reinforces that no one could invade the priestly office, which required continuous permanence and diligence.

The Levite count since a month old shows that they were numbered for a specific service; in addition, the observation about the firstborn surpluses explains why there was a ransom and why the money was collected on their behalf.

questions: What does Nadab and Abiú's death teach about the difference between religious zeal and real obedience to the word of God?
How does the separation of the Levites show that serving God is also a community responsibility, and not just an individual?
How does the idea of rescue in this chapter help to understand the biblical notion of belonging to the Lord and of substitution?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to reverence and order in the service to God. Examine whether his worship treats the saint as common, and if his life is willing to occupy the place God has given him, without envying foreign functions. It is also worth preaching: all that belongs to the LORD has been preserved by his mercy, and this must produce humility, faithfulness and zeal in care of the work of God and with the community of faith.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explain how the practical collection of the 273 rescues was made, and the commentators' notes present only additional hypotheses or details about this process. There is also not enough basis here to state with certainty what was the exact age of the Levites fit in full service, only that they were counted from one month of age for registration and belonging purposes. The Christian reading of Christ as typological fulfillment is interpretive and does not replace the immediate meaning of the chapter.
